entries.clue: Pain he’s displaced, looking fit? (2,5)

indicatorNotes.displaced: Something displaced has been shoved out of the place it belongs, and letters shoved out of place spell something else.

blocks.note: seven letters of fodder, the ache and the man who has it

annotation.surface: A man whose ache has shifted somewhere else, and who looks well on it.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'he’s' is not a letter, so only the seven spoken ones count. 'Displaced' covers the surface's wandering pain and the letters' reshuffle at the same time.
annotation.definitionFit: looking fit → IN SHAPE: being in shape is being in good physical condition, the everyday way of saying a body is trim and working well.

entries.clue: Born failure prone to roam around house (2-5)

indicatorNotes.to roam: To roam is to wander with no fixed route, and letters told to wander finish up somewhere other than where they started.
indicatorNotes.around: What goes around a thing encircles it, so the pair named next is shut inside the letters on either side.

blocks.note: the five letters of PRONE rearranged
ho. is the estate agent's short form of house

annotation.surface: A man born to fail who cannot settle, drifting about the house.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Prone' plays two parts at once: lying flat in the surface, and 'liable to' in the phrase that carries the instruction. The hyphen falls exactly where the house is slotted in.
annotation.definitionFit: Born failure → NO-HOPER: a no-hoper is written off before starting, the one nobody gives any chance of ever coming good.

entries.clue: Hour with advantage in boundary of a field (5)

blocks.note: h is the standard short form of hour, as on any timetable
to have the edge on a rival is to hold the advantage over them

annotation.surface: An hour's head start granted at the far side of a field.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boundary of a field' sounds like an instruction to take an outside letter; it is the thing itself, named straight. H for hour is a quiet abbreviation worth banking.
annotation.definitionFit: boundary of a field → HEDGE: hedges are what divide one English field from the next, the planted line marking where a farm's land stops.

entries.clue: Appropriate opening for snooker or features of the game? (7)

indicatorNotes.opening for: An opening is the way in at the front, so the letter taken is the one the following word starts with.

blocks.note: to pocket something is to take it for yourself, which is what appropriating it means
the opening letter of the word

annotation.surface: A suitable way to break at snooker, or the things that make the game what it is.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' reads as an adjective meaning suitable, sitting in front of 'opening'; it is the verb, and the verb is what a thief does. The question mark admits the definition is a description rather than a synonym.
annotation.definitionFit: features of the game → POCKETS: the six holes cut into the corners and sides of a snooker table are what the whole game is played into.

entries.clue: Humble Charles in brief facing figure (7)

indicatorNotes.in brief: In brief means put shortly, so the name arrives as the clipped version friends would use.
indicatorNotes.facing: To face a thing is to stand in front of it, so these letters take up the front of the answer and the rest follow.

blocks.note: Chas is the everyday shortening of Charles
a figure is a numeral, and ten is one of them written out

annotation.surface: A modest Charles standing in front of a shadowy figure.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Humble' reads as a description of Charles until you need it as a verb. 'Figure' is a number here, not a shape looming in the dark.
annotation.definitionFit: Humble → CHASTEN: both are verbs for taking somebody down a peg, the pride knocked out of them by a rebuke or a setback.

entries.clue: Kindly chap found in shade (6)

indicatorNotes.found in: Something found in a place was inside it all along, so the chap sits within the letters that follow rather than beside them.

blocks.note: a hue is a shade of colour
chap is the British word for a man

annotation.surface: A kindly fellow discovered standing in the shade.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shade' offers two pictures at once, the cool patch under a tree and a tint on a colour chart. Only the second one hands over letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Kindly → HUMANE: humane treatment is treatment that spares suffering, which is what acting kindly towards a person or an animal amounts to.

entries.clue: Reduce movement in slow dance (5,4)

indicatorNotes.movement in: Movement in something is a stirring of what lies inside it, and letters stirred about no longer stand where they did.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder, the dance itself

annotation.surface: Cutting down on how much movement a slow dance involves.
annotation.walkthrough: A slow dance has barely any movement in it to begin with, which is what makes the instruction read as description. 'Reduce' stands alone at the front, where a one-word definition is easiest to walk past.
annotation.definitionFit: Reduce → SCALE DOWN: to scale something down is to make it smaller by a set proportion, the standard phrase for cutting back a plan or a workforce.

entries.clue: Carry out piece of meat in old container for Elaine (7)

indicatorNotes.in: What is in a thing sits inside it, so the meat is slipped between the letters already found rather than added after them.
indicatorNotes.container for: A container is nothing but the outside of what it holds, so only the outer letters of the name that follows are kept.

blocks.note: ex- is the prefix for former, as in ex-wife or ex-champion
the first and last letters of ELAINE, the outside that would hold her
a cut is a joint or portion of meat as the butcher sells it

annotation.surface: A piece of meat kept in an old tin that belongs to Elaine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Container for' is no vessel at all but an instruction: keep the outside of the name and throw the middle away. 'Carry out' means perform, the way an order is carried out.
annotation.definitionFit: Carry out → EXECUTE: to execute an order, a plan or a manoeuvre is to carry it through, the sense with nothing to do with the scaffold.

entries.clue: Potential sort to alter place with pumps? (6,7)

indicatorNotes.to alter: To alter a thing is to change the way it is put together, and the letters beside the word come out put together differently.

blocks.note: thirteen letters of fodder, the promising character described

annotation.surface: A promising sort setting out to change somewhere fitted with pumps.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder is exactly as long as the answer, so nothing else in the clue can be contributing. 'Pumps' are flat shoes as well as the things on a forecourt, which is what the question mark trades on.
annotation.definitionFit: place with pumps → PETROL STATION: the pumps on the forecourt are the reason anyone pulls in, so naming them names the place.

entries.clue: Place to store tools in posh edifice (4)

indicatorNotes.in: What is in a phrase is already written out there, so the answer lies unbroken inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: the letters run across the join, from the end of the first word into the start of the second

annotation.surface: A place for the tools somewhere inside a rather grand building.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Posh' is the bait: it normally points at U or at some smart word, and here does neither. A four-letter hiding place is easiest to find straddling the gap between two words.
annotation.definitionFit: Place to store tools → SHED: the garden shed is where British households keep the spade, the mower and everything else with a handle.

entries.clue: Possibly make scarce dessert items (5,5)

indicatorNotes.Possibly: Possibly allows that the letters might fall one way or another, and that licence to fall differently is the whole instruction.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder, the phrase for taking yourself off

annotation.surface: Somebody quietly making the puddings disappear from the table.
annotation.walkthrough: To make yourself scarce is to slip away, and the same phrase supplies every letter here. 'Possibly' is the mildest anagram signal in the business, easy to read as padding.
annotation.definitionFit: dessert items → CREAM CAKES: cream cakes are the filled and piped things off a tea trolley, eaten as pudding rather than as a course.

entries.clue: Area of activity is special in this place (6)

blocks.note: sp. is the written short form of special, as on a pub's specials board
here means in this place and nowhere else

annotation.surface: A line of work that counts as special in this particular town.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Is' holds the two halves apart and carries nothing, which is what keeps the definition at the front hard to isolate. The answer is wanted in its figurative sense, a sphere of influence rather than a ball.
annotation.definitionFit: Area of activity → SPHERE: a person's sphere is the field they move and work in, as in a sphere of influence or the private sphere.

entries.clue: Junior in office ahead is one trailing winner (6-2)

blocks.note: an office runner is the youngster sent out with the messages
a side that is two up in a match is two ahead on the score

annotation.surface: An office junior out in front of the man who finished second.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Up' for ahead comes off the scoreboard: two up, three up with four to play. The definition describes second place without once using the word.
annotation.definitionFit: one trailing winner → RUNNER-UP: the runner-up is the competitor who came in immediately behind the winner, second in the final placings.

entries.clue: Relics, yep, for sorting out in an exact fashion (9)

indicatorNotes.for sorting out: Sorting a heap out means going through it and laying things down in a different order, which is what becomes of these letters.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder, the old objects and the casual agreement

annotation.surface: A heap of old relics, yes, that badly needs sorting out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Yep' is there only to supply letters, which is why it sits behind a comma looking like a shrug. The definition is an adverb phrase, so the answer has to be an adverb.
annotation.definitionFit: in an exact fashion → PRECISELY: to do a thing precisely is to do it exactly, the adverb for hitting a mark with no margin at all.

entries.clue: Amenable one in factory supporting committee (9)

indicatorNotes.in: What is in a thing is inside it, so the single letter named lands among the letters of the word that follows.
indicatorNotes.supporting: Whatever supports a load holds it up from underneath, and in a down entry that puts these letters below the rest.

blocks.note: com. is the short form of committee on an agenda or a letterhead
a plant is an industrial works, as in a car plant
one written as the Roman numeral

annotation.surface: An agreeable worker in a factory that answers to a committee.
annotation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'supporting' is a position rather than praise: the committee sits on top and the factory props it up. 'Plant' is the industrial sense, nothing growing.
annotation.definitionFit: Amenable → COMPLIANT: both describe somebody who goes along with what is asked without arguing, a compliant witness or an amenable child.

entries.clue: Currently fashionable article in Marbella, site for tourists (5)

blocks.note: a hot ticket or a hot band is the one everybody wants at this moment
Marbella is a resort on the Spanish coast, and the Spanish for 'the' is el

annotation.surface: A newspaper article about Marbella, the place tourists are flocking to.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Article' is the grammarian's word for 'a' or 'the', and naming a foreign town says which language to take it from. The piece of journalism is the decoy.
annotation.definitionFit: site for tourists → HOTEL: a hotel is where visitors put up for the night, the fixed point a tourist's stay is built around.

entries.clue: Crazy British group of soldiers (5)

blocks.note: B is the scoreboard and passport abbreviation for British
an army is a country's soldiers taken together

annotation.surface: A British regiment that has gone completely mad.
annotation.walkthrough: England's travelling cricket supporters have a famous nickname made of exactly these two pieces. The first half is old slang for mad, taken from barm, the froth on fermenting ale.
annotation.definitionFit: Crazy → BARMY: barmy is the everyday British word for someone soft in the head, as in a barmy idea or going barmy.

entries.clue: This tea is brewed for non-believer (7)

indicatorNotes.is brewed: Leaves left to brew swirl about in the pot, and letters told to brew end up just as stirred up.

blocks.note: seven letters of fodder, the pot standing in front of you

annotation.surface: A pot of tea left to stand, made for somebody who believes in nothing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'This' is fodder rather than a pointer back at the clue's own words, which is the easy thing to miss. 'For' joins the two halves and carries no letters of its own.
annotation.definitionFit: non-believer → ATHEIST: an atheist holds that no god exists, so the word for one who does not believe lands squarely on them.

entries.clue: Handle in a theatre? (5,4)

blocks.note: on the surface a grip or lever you take hold of; in the answer, slang for what a person goes by
on the surface where the fitting is screwed on; in the answer, the profession an assumed name is adopted for

annotation.surface: A grip or lever fitted somewhere inside a playhouse.
annotation.walkthrough: No letters change hands anywhere in this one. 'Handle' is the whole trick, the CB-radio sense of a name you go by doing duty for the ironmongery the theatre invites you to picture.
annotation.definitionFit: Handle in a theatre → STAGE NAME: a handle is informally what somebody is called, and the one an actor is called professionally is their stage name.

entries.clue: Set to receive free gift shortly? Come off it! (3,4)

indicatorNotes.to receive: To receive something is to take it in, so what is named next goes inside the letters already found.
indicatorNotes.shortly: Shortly means cut short, so the word beside it turns up with its last letter docked.

blocks.note: a liquid that has gelled has set, thickening into a jelly
a treat is a pleasure laid on at somebody else's expense, and its final letter is dropped

annotation.surface: Somebody all set to receive a free gift any minute now.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Set' looks like readiness or a television and is neither; it is the verb for a jelly firming up. 'Free gift' is the advertiser's phrase, two words for a thing somebody else pays for.
annotation.definitionFit: Come off it! → GET REAL: both are snapped at someone talking nonsense, telling them to drop the pretence and face how things actually are.

entries.clue: Way of working by conservative monarch, given to derision? (7)

blocks.note: MO is modus operandi, the detective's phrase for a criminal's usual way of working
C is the ballot-paper abbreviation for a Conservative candidate
a king is a reigning monarch

annotation.surface: The habitual methods of a cautious monarch with a taste for sneering.
annotation.walkthrough: Lower-case 'conservative' reads as cautiousness rather than the party, which is what keeps the single letter out of sight. A capital would have given it away.
annotation.definitionFit: given to derision → MOCKING: a mocking tone or a mocking laugh is one that jeers at its target, which is derision turned into a habit.

entries.clue: Photo cooking ending in pleasant stew (6)

indicatorNotes.cooking: Cooking breaks a thing down and puts it back together in another form, which is what happens to the letters beside it.
indicatorNotes.ending in: The ending of a word is its final letter, so only the last letter of the one named is taken.

blocks.note: five letters of fodder
the last letter of PLEASANT, thrown in with the jumble

annotation.surface: A photograph of something on the hob that turns into a pleasant stew.
annotation.walkthrough: A Lancashire hotpot is lamb and onion under a lid of sliced potato, baked slowly, which is the dish the definition wants. 'Ending in' points forward at 'pleasant' rather than back at the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: stew → HOTPOT: a hotpot is meat and vegetables cooked slowly together in one pot, which is exactly what a stew is.

entries.clue: Spend first part of holiday in very popular event (5,3)

indicatorNotes.first part of: The first part of a word is where it begins, so its opening letter is all that gets taken.
indicatorNotes.in: What is in something sits inside it, so that letter is planted among the letters of what follows.

blocks.note: an event that is a sell-out has had every ticket taken
the opening letter of HOLIDAY

annotation.surface: Money spent on the first part of a holiday at an event everyone wants tickets for.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spend' stands alone at the front doing the whole job of definition, which is how one-word definitions hide. The holiday's letter drops in immediately after the S.
annotation.definitionFit: Spend → SHELL OUT: to shell out is to hand money over, usually more of it than you meant to, the informal phrase for paying up.

entries.clue: Three in Italy start to notice champion in depression (6)

indicatorNotes.start to: The start of a word is its first letter, so only the opening of the word that follows is used.

blocks.note: tre is the Italian for three, and naming the country says which language to count in
the first letter of NOTICE
Ch. is the title printed before a champion's name in a pedigree or a show catalogue

annotation.surface: Three people in Italy beginning to spot a champion down in a hollow.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In Italy' is the instruction to count in Italian, a habit worth picking up: a country named next to a number nearly always means translate it. The definition is a dug hollow, not a slump in trade.
annotation.definitionFit: depression → TRENCH: a trench is a long narrow hollow cut into the ground, which is a depression in the plain geographical sense.

entries.clue: Avoid introduction lacking in publicity (5)

indicatorNotes.lacking in: Something lacking in a quality has none of it at all, so the letters named next are taken out of the word before them.

blocks.note: an introduction to a piece of music is its prelude
PR is public relations, the trade of getting publicity, and the pair comes off the front

annotation.surface: An opening act that got no press coverage whatsoever.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lacking in publicity' reads as a grumble about poor promotion and works as a subtraction. The two letters come off the front, which is where an introduction's own opening sits.
annotation.definitionFit: Avoid → ELUDE: to elude a pursuer is to keep slipping out of their reach, the evasive kind of avoidance rather than simply not doing something.

entries.clue: Regard unfavourably vapid prose requiring editing (10)

indicatorNotes.requiring editing: Writing that needs editing has to be cut about and put back in another order, which is what becomes of these letters.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder, the dull writing itself

annotation.surface: A reader taking a dim view of flat writing that badly needs an edit.
annotation.walkthrough: Definition and fodder describe the same act of criticism, so the clue reads as one unbroken sentence. 'Vapid' means flat and flavourless, the sort of prose an editor reaches for the pencil over.
annotation.definitionFit: Regard unfavourably → DISAPPROVE: to disapprove of a thing is to take a poor view of it, judging it wrong or not good enough.

entries.clue: Component in military squad (4)

blocks.note: one of the separate parts a larger whole is built out of
the army's word for a body of troops organised to work as one

annotation.surface: A part fitted somewhere inside an army squad.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' is the join, not an instruction to put anything inside anything: two senses are simply laid end to end. The same four letters cover a part of a machine and a body of soldiers.
annotation.definitionFit: A component is one unit of a larger assembly; in the forces a unit is a named formation such as a platoon or a battalion.

entries.clue: Decree with time accepted by David, say (7)

indicatorNotes.accepted by: To accept a thing is to take it in, so the letter named is let inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: Michelangelo's David is a statue, so the name stands as one instance of the thing
t is the standard short form of time

annotation.surface: A ruling that David, given time, was prepared to accept.
annotation.walkthrough: 'David, say' is definition by example: the comma and 'say' warn that one particular David stands in for the whole class. The inserted letter lands beside the last, which hides the seam.
annotation.definitionFit: Decree → STATUTE: a statute is a law formally laid down by a legislature, a decree once it has been written into the books.

entries.clue: Friend embracing poor Reg showing hypersensitivity? (7)

indicatorNotes.embracing: To embrace someone is to get your arms right round them, so the letters named next finish up enclosed.
indicatorNotes.poor: Something poor is in a sorry state, and letters in a sorry state are not standing in the order they ought to be.

blocks.note: an ally is a friend, the one who is on your side
the three letters of the name rearranged

annotation.surface: A friend throwing their arms around poor Reg, who is clearly in a state.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Poor Reg' is sympathy on the surface and an instruction underneath: the man is in a bad way and so are his letters. The embrace opens the friend up, leaving one letter stranded at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: hypersensitivity → ALLERGY: an allergy is the immune system overreacting to something harmless, which is hypersensitivity in its medical sense.
